newsitem.title: USA: Enzyme may have potential against cancer cells.
newsitem.headline: Enzyme may have potential against cancer cells.

text.p: California researchers said Thursday they had identified an enzyme that interacts with a crucial cancer-causing gene and may hold out promise for new ways of fighting cancer.

The research, reported in Friday's edition of the journal Science, has only been done so far on yeast and not tested on human cells, so it is far too soon to know whether it will be safe and effective in people.

Still, scientists say it is a key discovery because the enzyme interacts with a protein made by the ras gene. That gene is believed to be the second-most-common cancer-causing gene in people and has been linked to colon, lung, pancreatic and liver cancers.

"Ras has been the focus of much scientific research beause of its role in cancers which are difficult to treat," said Matthew Ashby, director of biology at the privately held Acacia Biosciences in Richmond, Calif. Ashby worked with scientists at the University of California at Berkeley on the seven-year hunt for the enzyme.
Ras's job is to tell a cell whether to divide or not. A flawed or mutated ras gene tells cells to divide and divide and divide, the uncontrolled growth that causes cancer.

But by removing this particular enzyme, ras activity plummeted and cells returned to normal. The goal now is to use this finding to discover how to eliminate ras's harmful properties in human cells, while preserving its necessary functions.
Although yeast is a much simpler organism than a human being, many of its genes have human counterparts so it is a good model for drug studies.
